title: Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP)
subtitle: Resect between the bladder neck and the verumontanum, and watch the fluid

sources.title: EAU Guidelines on Management of Non-neurogenic Male Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Lower urinary tract symptoms in men: management (CG97)

indications: Moderate to severe lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic obstruction that are bothersome despite, or unsuitable for, medical therapy.
Absolute indications: refractory urinary retention, recurrent infection, bladder stones, recurrent haematuria from the prostate, or upper tract dilatation and renal impairment from obstruction.
Prostate volume in the mid-range is the classic TURP territory; very large glands may be better served by enucleation or open or robotic simple prostatectomy.
contraindications: Uncorrected coagulopathy or anticoagulation that cannot be safely managed peri-operatively.
Detrusor underactivity without obstruction, where resection will not restore voiding; establish the diagnosis with urodynamics when in doubt.
Suspected prostate cancer that has not been staged and discussed.
preparation: Symptom score, flow rate and post-void residual; urodynamics where the diagnosis is uncertain (younger men, neurological disease, low flow with low residual, previous failed surgery).
Sterile urine before surgery; treat a positive culture, and give culture-directed prophylaxis in catheterised men.
Plan anticoagulant and antiplatelet management with the prescribing team.

Consent must cover retrograde ejaculation, bleeding and transfusion, infection, TUR syndrome, urethral stricture, bladder neck contracture, incontinence, erectile dysfunction, failure to void, and the need for further treatment.
Prostate-specific antigen and cancer assessment when the result would change management.
positioning: Lithotomy with the hips flexed and abducted, the buttocks just over the end of the table, and both legs supported in padded stirrups.
Spinal anaesthesia is commonly used and lets the anaesthetist detect early confusion from fluid absorption.
equipment: Continuous-flow resectoscope with 30 degree lens; monopolar (glycine) or bipolar (saline) generator and loops.
Urethral sounds or Otis urethrotome; Ellik evacuator.
Three-way catheter and irrigation set; a fluid-balance chart for the irrigant.
Point-of-care sodium measurement available in theatre for monopolar cases.
anatomy: The verumontanum marks the distal limit of resection. The external urethral sphincter lies just distal to it, and resection beyond it causes incontinence.
The ureteric orifices lie close to the bladder neck, especially with a large median lobe that hides them.
The prostatic capsule is seen as a fibrous layer of circular fibres; fat or large venous sinuses beyond it mean the capsule has been breached.
The bladder neck is at roughly the 6 o'clock position on the floor, with lateral lobes at 3 and 9 and the median lobe protruding into the bladder.
criticalSafety: Identify the verumontanum before the first cut and recheck it repeatedly. Never resect distal to it.
Identify both ureteric orifices before resecting a median lobe.
Monopolar resection: watch the fluid. Opened venous sinuses and capsular perforation increase absorption; finish quickly and tell the anaesthetist if either is seen.
Confusion, restlessness, visual disturbance, nausea, hypertension then hypotension, or bradycardia during or after a monopolar TURP is TUR syndrome until a sodium says otherwise.
structuresAtRisk: Prostatic capsule and periprostatic venous plexus
Rectum (deep posterior resection at the apex)
commonErrors: Losing orientation and resecting distal to the verumontanum.
Undermining the trigone at the bladder neck, so the catheter tip passes under it.
Over-deep resection of the bladder neck in a small gland, leading to bladder neck contracture.
Chasing a bleeding sinus at high pressure while absorbing irrigant.
Continuing a long monopolar resection after a capsular perforation.
complications: Bleeding, clot retention and transfusion, early or secondary.
TUR syndrome: dilutional hyponatraemia and fluid overload from irrigant absorption with monopolar resection; much less frequent with bipolar saline resection.
Capsular perforation with extravasation; bladder perforation.
Retrograde ejaculation (common), urethral stricture, bladder neck contracture, incontinence, erectile dysfunction.
Urinary infection and sepsis; failure to void after catheter removal.
postop: Continuous irrigation until the effluent is clear, with strict recording of irrigant in and out.
Check serum sodium after any monopolar TURP with prolonged resection, perforation or new symptoms.

Treat TUR syndrome by stopping absorption, restricting fluid, a loop diuretic for overload, and hypertonic saline for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia per local protocol in a monitored setting; avoid over-rapid correction.
Trial without catheter usually within a few days; warn about haematuria and secondary bleeding around the second week.
Review histology and discuss any incidental cancer at the multidisciplinary meeting.

steps.emphasis: State the energy platform and the irrigation fluid aloud at the time-out. The fluid is a safety decision, not a nursing detail.
Sterile urine before resection; culture-directed prophylaxis for catheterised men.
Lithotomy with padded stirrups and both legs raised and lowered together. Check the common peroneal nerve at the lateral knee.
Map the verumontanum, the lobes, the bladder neck and both ureteric orifices before any resection.
Weigh the resected tissue; the weight goes in the operative note.
Coagulate arterial bleeders at low irrigation pressure. Venous sinus ooze is best managed by finishing the resection and catheter traction, not by prolonged diathermy.

step.turp.median-lobe.title: Bladder neck and median lobe
step.turp.median-lobe.why: A median lobe hides the ureteric orifices and the trigone. Resecting it first opens the channel for the irrigant and improves the view for the rest of the operation.
how: Identify both ureteric orifices before starting, then resect the median lobe in controlled strokes from the bladder neck towards the verumontanum.
Develop a channel at the 6 o'clock position down to the circular fibres of the bladder neck, but no deeper.
Keep the loop moving in a controlled arc; withdraw the whole resectoscope rather than the loop alone for long strokes.
pitfalls: Undermining the trigone by resecting too deep at the bladder neck.
Resecting a ureteric orifice hidden by a large median lobe.

step.turp.lateral-lobes.title: Lateral lobes
step.turp.lateral-lobes.why: Systematic resection of each lateral lobe down to the capsule removes the obstructing tissue while keeping orientation and haemostasis manageable.
how: Resect each lateral lobe from the bladder neck towards the apex, working from 12 o'clock downwards or from the floor upwards per the surgeon's method, and stay consistent.
Stop at the capsule: circular white fibres. Fat or large open sinuses mean you are through it.
Coagulate arterial bleeders as you go to keep the field clear.
pitfalls: Chasing tissue into the capsule on one side while the other lobe is still obstructing.
Opening large venous sinuses early in a monopolar case.

step.turp.apex.title: Apical resection, staying proximal to the verumontanum
step.turp.apex.why: The apex is where continence is won or lost. The external sphincter sits just distal to the verumontanum, and most post-TURP stress incontinence follows apical over-resection.
how: Re-identify the verumontanum and keep it in view while resecting apical tissue on each side.
Use short, shallow strokes at the apex and never start a stroke distal to the verumontanum.
Withdraw the scope into the bulbar urethra and look back to confirm an open channel and an intact sphincter.
pitfalls: Resecting the verumontanum itself, losing the landmark.
A deep posterior apical cut towards the rectum.

step.turp.fluid-watch.title: TUR syndrome watch: time, pressure, sinuses and sodium
step.turp.fluid-watch.why: Irrigant absorption is silent until it is dangerous. Resection time, irrigation pressure, open venous sinuses and capsular perforation all increase it, and the awake spinal patient is the best monitor.
how: Tell the anaesthetist the start time of resection and update them on sinuses or perforation.
Keep the irrigation pressure as low as gives a clear view; empty the bladder regularly with an intermittent-flow scope.
On any symptom or sign (confusion, nausea, visual disturbance, hypertension then hypotension, bradycardia), stop resecting, achieve haemostasis, finish, and check sodium and osmolality.
Prefer bipolar saline resection for large glands or long cases where it is available.
pitfalls: Assuming the restless patient needs more sedation rather than a sodium.
Giving intravenous fluid for the subsequent hypotension in a patient who is already overloaded.
